subject: Nicholas of Myra
note: One writer, research and writing in one pass (SAINT-BRIEF.md). Every fetched text is under design/saints-hub/sources/people/nicholas-of-myra/ (gitignored). The record is thin in facts and rich in stories: the page names each story's first written source and its date. Modern copyrighted works (Lendering, Pearse, Jerman, Jones, the OCA, Britannica, the Episcopal Church) are used for facts and datings, and quoted only in a few short lines as each side's own words.

life.text: Scarcely anything historically certain except that he was bishop of Myra in the 4th century; died 6 December, 345 or 352; his name not in any of the old lists of Nicaea's bishops; Justinian built a church in his honour at Constantinople; his name occurs in the liturgy ascribed to Chrysostom; patron of mariners, merchants, bakers, travellers, children, and of Greece and Russia; relics at Bari with the oily substance called Manna di S. Nicola.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), St. Nicholas of Myra (Michael Ott)

life.text: The Golden Legend's chapter: birth at Patara to Epiphanes and Johane, fasting as a baby on Wednesdays and Fridays, the three dowries, election at matins, the sailors in the storm, the grain ships, Diana's tree and burning oil, the three innocents and the three princes (Nepotian, Ursyn, Apollyn), the dream of Constantine, death with Psalm 31 in 343, oil from the tomb, forty-seven knights of Bari and four monks in 1087, later miracles (the Jew's staff, the image, the boy strangled by the devil, the golden cup, Adeodatus).
life.source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton (1483), ed. F. S. Ellis (1900), Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

life.text: Dating of the Lives and stories: Proclus's encomium (late per Anrich); Theodore Anagnostes' Historia Tripartita in a 13th-century manuscript names Nicholas at Nicaea (Anrich: interpolation; Cioffari: authentic); Life of Nicholas of Sion, about 564, refers to the tomb of Nicholas of Myra, and was later mixed into his Life; Praxis de stratelatis (Anrich 460 to 580; Cioffari before the mid-400s); Michael the Archimandrite (Anrich 814 to 843; Cioffari about 700); Nicetas of Paphlagonia, before 890, first mention of Nicaea; a synaxarium Life of about 900 adds prison under the last persecution and Nicaea; Vita Compilata 860 to 975 intertwines the two Nicholases; Metaphrastes 975 to 1000; at least 50 legends in the thousand years after his death; Golden Legend and Petrus de Natalibus follow John the Deacon.
life.source: Roger Pearse, Literary development of the Life of St Nicholas, summarising Aart Blom, Nikolaas van Myra en zijn tijd (1998), appendix 2

life.text: Michael's Life summarised (Patara, chastity, fasting infant, inheritance given away, dowries, temple of Artemis destroyed, three generals, sailors, famine); Apollonius of Tyana parallels (dowry, saving the condemned, bilocation); Anrich (1913, 1917) held the real Nicholas lost; Cioffari (1987) and Blom (1998) found the topography reliable; Myra's temple of Artemis (coin of Gordian III); granaries of the famine story excavated at Andriake; original tomb outside the walls, where Roman law still forbade burial inside cities in the early 300s; the church still stands; of eleven medieval copies of the Nicaea list, three name Nicholas, one of them among the best; Lendering concludes the dowry story is simply true.
life.source: Jona Lendering, Early Evidence (from Livius), St. Nicholas Center

life.text: The slap: first in Petrus de Natalibus (bishop of Equilio from 1370, died about 1400), Catalogus sanctorum: 'Fertur beatum Nicolaum jam senem Nicaeno concilio interfuisse et quemdam Arrianum zelo fidei in maxillam percussisse', deprived of mitre and pallium, 'propter quod ut plurimum sine mitra depingitur'; Arius himself first in Damaskenos the Monk's Life (Thesaurus, oldest edition Venice 1570); the Greek word means a slap; the scene is in Dionysius of Fourna's painter's manual and in icons. Anrich, Hagios Nikolaos (1913), vol. 1 p. 459.
life.source: Roger Pearse, Did St Nicholas of Myra punch Arius at the Council of Nicaea? (2015)

life.text: The Orthodox life: Patara, Theophanes and Nonna, the dowries in secret ('always strove to do this secretly'), Holy Sion founded by his uncle (from Nicholas of Sion), chosen by vision, prison under Diocletian, at Nicaea 'struck him upon the face', restored by Christ and the Mother of God with Gospel and omophorion, the three men and the officers, relics to Bari 1087.
life.source: OCA, Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, 6 December

life.text: The translation: merchants of Bari returning from Antioch; four monks; forty-seven armed men; 300 gold coins refused; monks bound; sarcophagus full of myrrh opened 20 April 1087; crowd at the shore too late; arrived 8 May, carried into St Stephen's 9 May; church consecrated by Urban II; 9 May kept first only at Bari; the Greek Church did not keep it, regarding the loss 'as a sad event'; the Russian Church established the feast; the Russian Church honours him every Thursday; the men of Bari decided 'to save the relics of Saint Nicholas'.
life.source: OCA, Translation of the Relics of St Nicholas, 9 May

life.text: Coptic account for 10 Kiahk: from Myra ('Mora'), parents Epiphanius and Tona, dowries of 100 dinars three times, tortured by Diocletian 'severely for many years', wrote to his church from prison, 'one of the 318 fathers' at Nicaea, bishop more than 40 years, lived about 80 years; footnote: 'the true personality behind the story of St. Claus or Baba Noel'.
life.source: Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk, CopticChurch.net

life.text: Butler: the Greek histories agree on imprisonment and Nicaea, 'The silence of other authors make many justly suspect these circumstances'; the Muscovites' veneration; 'no saint was more universally honoured in all Christian nations'; the raid 'could only be justified by the laws of a just war'; landed at Bari 9 May 1087.
life.source: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints (1756 to 1759), 1866 edition, 6 December, St. Nicholas Center transcription

life.text: Justinian 'established a shrine to St. Priscus and St. Nicholas, an entirely new creation of his own' on the Golden Horn near Blachernae.
life.source: Procopius, Buildings, Book 1, chapter 6, tr. H. B. Dewing (1940), LacusCurtius
life.note: Procopius does not say which Nicholas; the Catholic Encyclopedia, Britannica and the Episcopal Church take Justinian's church as his.

life.text: Dante: the largess which Nicholas gave the maidens, praised by Hugh Capet on the terrace of avarice.
life.source: Dante, Purgatorio, canto 20, tr. Longfellow (1867), Wikisource

life.text: The three boys: not in the early Greek legends, the Golden Legend or the Roman breviary; in Latin hymns of the 11th century; a Latin play of about 1100 from Hildesheim (a British Library manuscript, per Joel Fredell); Wace's French Life of about 1150, verses 213 to 226, 'Tres clercs alouent a escole'; later the butcher and the salting tub (Southern English Legendary); the most popular miracle in art; McKnight (1917) quoting Wace on schoolboys keeping the day.
life.source: Roger Pearse, St Nicholas and the story of the three schoolboys (2019), after Joel Fredell, Charles W. Jones and George McKnight

life.text: Relics: bulk in Bari since 1087; some in San Nicolò al Lido, Venice, as many as 500 fragments, found by an anatomical study to complement Bari's; a pelvis fragment (left pubis) owned by Fr Dennis O'Neill, Morton Grove, Illinois, from Lyon, radiocarbon dated to the 4th century; Bari has the left ilium; Higham: science can only prove it is not.
life.source: University of Oxford press release, 5 December 2017, via EurekAlert

life.text: The manna: drawn each 9 May since 1980 by the rector before the Pope's delegate, the Archbishop of Bari and an Orthodox bishop; no more than about 50 ml a year; the Greeks call it myron; mixed with blessed water and bottled; the casket proven impermeable, so infiltration excluded (Fr Gerardo Cioffari, Centro Studi Nicolaiani).
life.source: St. Nicholas Center, Devotion and Use of Manna, from the Centro Studi Nicolaiani, Bari

life.text: The manna found to be water by scientists at the University of Bari in 1925, in all likelihood condensation (tomb underground in a port city); extracted each May since 1980; Venice's relics do not produce it; the Seljuq Turks invaded Anatolia in 1071.
life.source: Britannica, Do the Relics of Saint Nicholas Really Emit a Holy Substance?

life.text: Britannica: nothing certain known; buried at Myra, shrine known by the 6th century; boy bishop on his feast until Holy Innocents' Day; after the Reformation his cult survived only in Holland as Sinterklaas; Dutch colonists took it to New Amsterdam, adopted as Santa Claus.
life.source: Britannica, St. Nicholas

life.text: Irving's History of New York (1809): St Nicholas the patron of New Amsterdam; the passages on gifts, the treetops and the finger beside the nose are in the later text (Jerman: added in the 1812 edition).
life.source: Washington Irving, Knickerbocker's History of New York (Conkey reprint of a later edition), Project Gutenberg 13042

life.text: Troy Sentinel, 23 December 1823: 'Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas', unsigned, with Orville Holley's preface naming 'Sante Claus'; the poem says St. Nicholas and St. Nick, eight reindeer including 'Dunder and Blixem', 'laying his finger aside of his nose'.
life.source: Wikisource, Troy Sentinel/1823/12/23

life.text: Charles W. Jones (1954): 'Without Irving there would be no Santa Claus'; no proof the Dutch colonists kept Sinterklaas. Tom A. Jerman (2020): Irving's gift-giver passages were added in 1812; Santa grew from German 'terror men' by way of the 1821 Children's Friend ('Santeclaus', a flying reindeer) and the 1823 poem; 'St. Nicholas and Santa Claus were two different characters'; by the mid-1800s the poem was acknowledged as Clement C. Moore's; Moore took the finger-beside-the-nose scene from Irving.
life.source: Tom A. Jerman, Revisiting the Knickerbocker Origin Story of Santa Claus, History News Network

life.text: Episcopal Church: very little known; the Arius story dates more than 1,000 years after his death; almost 400 churches in England dedicated to him; 'his name was brought to America by the Dutch colonists in New York'; feast 6 December, 'Nicholas of Myra, Bishop, c. 342'.
life.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

life.text: Pronunciation: Nicholas \ˈni-k(ə-)ləs\, Myra \ˈmī-rə\.
life.source: Merriam-Webster

could_not_verify: No public-domain English translation of Michael the Archimandrite's Life, the Praxis de stratelatis or Nicephorus's account of 1087 was found (the St. Nicholas Center's are modern): the page tells them in our words and quotes the Golden Legend.
The Russian Church's 19 December and 22 May are the Julian dates worked out, not read on a Russian page.
That Justinian's shrine of St Priscus and St Nicholas (Procopius) was for Nicholas of Myra is the common reading, not stated by Procopius.
Whether the finger-beside-the-nose scene was already in Irving's 1809 text: the page says only that it is in the text read today, and that Irving added the gift passages from 1812 (Jerman).
The 1773 New York newspaper note on 'St. A Claus' and John Pintard's 1810 broadside were left out: no primary text was fetched.
The 2004 facial reconstruction and the Gemile island tomb theory were left out: no source beyond Wikipedia was fetched.

checked: Every number and date against the texts on disk: the 3 throws, 47 men and 4 monks, 300 gold coins, 20 April / 8 May / 9 May 1087, 50 ml of manna (stnc-manna.txt), 1925 and 1980 (Britannica, St. Nicholas Center), 343 (Golden Legend), 345 or 352 (Catholic Encyclopedia), c. 326 (CofE) and c. 342 (LFF, ELCA), the Lives' datings (Pearse after Blom: Anrich and Cioffari), Theodore the Reader, 11 lists and 3 names (Lendering), 1370 and 1570 for the slap (Pearse), the three boys' first witnesses (Pearse), Irving 1809/1812, the 1821 booklet and the 1823 poem (Jerman, Troy Sentinel), the Oxford 2017 release.

Every feast in its calendar text: USCCB and Calendarium Romanum 1969 (6 December, the commentary on the depositio and the 900s), the 1916 Martyrology (9 May, 6 December), CofE, LFF, LSB, ELCA, OCA 6 December and 9 May, the Coptic 10 Kiahk.

Attributions: the Coptic synaxarium (parents, prison, 318 fathers, the Baba Noel footnote), the OCA (Theophanes and Nonna, secrecy, Holy Sion, the slap as tradition, the Thursday line, the 9 May account), Butler (in context), the Catholic Encyclopedia, Britannica, Lendering, Jerman and Jones.

changed: Bari raid: Butler's line was framed as a rebuke ('Even Alban Butler... thought'). His sentence goes on 'joined with the apprehension of the sacrilegious impiety of the Mahometans': he was defending the raid on those grounds. Now: he said it 'could only be justified by the laws of a just war', together with the fear that the Turks would profane the relics.

The slap myth: Lendering, cited elsewhere on the page, argues the other way ('this anecdote is embarrassing, and this is a reason why it is unlikely to have been invented'). His view is now added in his words, with an evidence entry (stnc-early-sources.txt), so the page does not pick a winner.
How he died: 'No record gives the year' contradicted the page's own 343 (Golden Legend) and 345 or 352 (Catholic Encyclopedia). Now 'No record from his own time gives the year.'
Nicholas of Sion 'who died about 564' (myth and circle): the text on disk dates his Life, not his death, to about 564. Now 'in the 500s', with the Life 'written about 564'.

Feast note: 'The Greek churches never took up 9 May' was stronger than the OCA ('the Greek Church did not establish the celebration'). Now 'The Greek Church did not take up 9 May.' Added the OCA's third date: 'The OCA also remembers his birth on 29 July' (oca-dec6.txt: 'commemorated ... on July 29 (his nativity)').
Election: 'The senior bishop' became 'The bishop who led the choosing' (the Golden Legend: 'a bishop of great authority, and all the election was in him').
Hub filter side: east and west became east only. The other pages mark where a person lived (both only for those who lived in both halves: Irenaeus, Justin, Cassian); Nicholas lived only in Lycia.
for_owner: Hub group: none of the eight groups fits him; filters.groups is empty. A group such as bishops or wonderworkers would be a lib/ change.
Repin's 1888 painting in the gallery shows a raised sword over a kneeling man in chains (Nicholas stopping the blow). It is not the band; your call whether it is too violent for the page.
Band file size: the cracked 1294 icon is 782 KB at 1154 x 1600, quality 82, against about 450 KB for other bands.
The boy carried home (Adeodatus) is called 'a later legend' and dated only by the Golden Legend of the 1260s; no text on disk gives its first telling.
